questions.question: Which protocol does SSH use to connect to a Linux EC2 instance?

explanation.correct: SSH (Secure Shell) is the protocol used to connect to Linux-based EC2 instances securely over the network.
explanation.why: HTTP is for web traffic, RDP is for Windows graphical desktops, FTP is for file transfer without encryption.

questions.question: What is the default port number for SSH connections?

explanation.correct: Port 22 is the standard well-known port for SSH. It must be open in the Security Group inbound rules.
explanation.why: Port 80 is HTTP, 443 is HTTPS, 3389 is RDP. These are all different protocols.

questions.question: Which EC2 connection method requires NO software installation and opens a terminal directly in the browser?

explanation.correct: EC2 Instance Connect is browser-based and requires no software — AWS handles the temporary key injection automatically.
explanation.why: PuTTY requires installation, SSH requires a terminal app, and RDP is for Windows only.

questions.question: What file format does PuTTY require for SSH key files — and what tool converts your AWS .pem file to that format?

explanation.correct: PuTTY uses .ppk (PuTTY Private Key) format. PuTTYgen is the companion tool included with PuTTY that converts .pem to .ppk.
explanation.why: AWS provides .pem files which are not directly usable by PuTTY without conversion.

questions.question: What permissions must you set on your .pem key file before SSH will accept it on Linux/Mac?

explanation.correct: chmod 400 sets the file as read-only for the owner only. SSH refuses to use key files with too-open permissions for security reasons.
explanation.why: chmod 777 (full access to everyone) and chmod 644 (readable by all) are too permissive — SSH will show 'Unprotected private key file' error.

questions.question: Which port must be open in the Security Group for RDP connections to a Windows EC2 instance?

explanation.correct: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) operates on port 3389. This must be added as an inbound rule in the Security Group.
explanation.why: Port 22 is SSH (Linux), 443 is HTTPS (web), 8080 is an alternate HTTP port.

questions.question: To connect to a Windows EC2 instance via RDP, what do you use your .pem key file for?

options.text: To establish the encrypted RDP tunnel
To decrypt and retrieve the Windows Administrator password
PEM files are not used with Windows instances

explanation.correct: The .pem private key is used to decrypt the encrypted Windows password that AWS stores on the instance. You paste this decrypted password into the RDP login dialog.
explanation.why: The .pem file does not directly establish the RDP connection — it is only used to reveal the password.

questions.question: What state must an EC2 instance be in before you can change its instance type?

explanation.correct: The instance must be in the Stopped state to change its instance type. You cannot resize a running instance.
explanation.why: AWS needs to deallocate and reallocate hardware resources, which requires the instance to be off.

questions.question: What happens to an EC2 instance's public IP address when you stop and then start it?

options.text: It is released and a new public IP is assigned
The IP is locked for 24 hours

explanation.correct: When you stop an instance, its public IPv4 address is released back to AWS. When you start it again, a new public IP is assigned from the pool.
explanation.why: To keep a static public IP across stop/start cycles, you must use an Elastic IP Address.

questions.question: Which EC2 pricing model can be interrupted by AWS with only 2 minutes' notice but offers up to 90% discount?

explanation.correct: Spot Instances use spare AWS capacity and offer massive discounts — but AWS can reclaim them with a 2-minute warning when the capacity is needed elsewhere.
explanation.why: Reserved Instances and Savings Plans offer discounts through commitment, not through interruptibility. On-Demand has no discount.

questions.question: You are running a production web application that must be available 24/7 for at least the next 2 years. Which pricing model gives the best savings?

explanation.correct: Reserved Instances offer up to 72% discount for 1 or 3-year commitments — ideal for predictable, steady-state production workloads.
explanation.why: On-Demand is most expensive, Spot can be interrupted (unsuitable for production web apps), Dedicated Host is most costly.

questions.question: What is the key difference between Termination Protection and Stop Protection?

options.text: Termination Protection prevents deletion; Stop Protection prevents the instance from being shut down
They are the same feature with different names
Stop Protection prevents deletion; Termination Protection prevents shutdown
Termination Protection only works on Windows; Stop Protection only works on Linux

explanation.correct: Termination Protection blocks permanent deletion (terminate action). Stop Protection blocks the stop action that shuts down the instance while keeping it recoverable.
explanation.why: They are independent, separate features that protect against different actions.

questions.question: During which EC2 instance state does billing for compute charges begin?

explanation.correct: Compute billing starts when the instance enters the Running state. Pending is a pre-billing transition state.
explanation.why: You are only charged for compute when the instance is actively running. Stopped instances still incur EBS storage charges but not compute charges.

questions.question: An EC2 instance is in the Stopped state. Which charges STILL apply?

explanation.correct: Stopping an instance halts compute charges, but attached EBS volumes persist and continue to be billed at the standard EBS storage rate.
explanation.why: EBS volumes exist independently of the instance state — they hold your data and must be paid for even when the instance is off.

questions.question: What is the difference in public IP behaviour between Rebooting an instance vs Stopping then Starting it?

options.text: Reboot releases the public IP; Stop/Start retains it
Reboot retains the public IP; Stop/Start releases it and assigns a new one
Both operations result in a new public IP
Neither operation affects the public IP

explanation.correct: Reboot keeps the instance on the same physical host with the same public IP. Stop/Start may move the instance to different hardware and always releases the old public IP.
explanation.why: This is a classic exam distinction — the only way to get a permanent public IP is an Elastic IP Address.

questions.question: A company must run a Windows workload on hardware that no other AWS customer shares, due to a software licensing audit requirement. Which pricing/hosting option should they use?

explanation.correct: Dedicated Hosts provide a physical server exclusively allocated to your account, with visibility into socket and core counts — required for per-core or per-socket software licensing compliance.
explanation.why: On-Demand, Spot, and Reserved Instances may share physical hardware with other AWS customers (multi-tenant).

questions.question: Which EC2 connection method temporarily injects a one-time SSH key into the instance for 60 seconds?

explanation.correct: EC2 Instance Connect generates a temporary one-time key, pushes it to the instance metadata for 60 seconds, then removes it — all transparently without exposing the key to the user.
explanation.why: PuTTY and SSH .pem methods use a persistent key pair created at launch time.

questions.question: What is the 'Instance initiated shutdown behavior' setting and what is the recommended production value?

options.text: Controls whether SSH or RDP is used; recommended value is SSH
Controls whether an OS shutdown command stops or terminates the instance; recommended production value is Stop
Controls the reboot timeout; recommended value is 60 seconds
Controls Auto Scaling behavior; recommended value is Terminate

explanation.correct: This setting defines what happens when a shutdown command is issued from inside the OS (e.g., sudo shutdown). Stop means the instance is stoppable and recoverable; Terminate means it is permanently deleted.
explanation.why: On production servers, always set to Stop — accidental termination from inside the OS is unrecoverable.

questions.question: You need to run a 48-hour data analysis job on EC2 that can be safely interrupted and resumed. The job will not run again for months after completion. Which pricing model is MOST cost-effective?

explanation.correct: Spot Instances are ideal — up to 90% cheaper than On-Demand, and since the batch job can be interrupted and restarted, the interruptibility risk is acceptable. Reserved Instances require a year's commitment for a job running 48 hours.
explanation.why: On-Demand is safe but expensive. Reserved requires commitment for infrequent use. Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive option.

questions.question: Your colleague says 'I stopped the EC2 instance so we are not paying anything now.' Is this accurate?

options.text: Yes — stopping an instance stops all charges
No — EBS storage charges continue even when the instance is stopped
No — compute charges continue at half rate when stopped
Yes — but only if you stopped it using the CLI, not the console

explanation.correct: Stopping an EC2 instance stops compute charges, but any attached EBS volumes continue to incur storage charges. Your colleague is partially correct but the statement is inaccurate.
explanation.why: EBS volumes persist independently — they hold your data and must be paid for regardless of instance state.

questions.question: A Savings Plan commits you to a specific amount of usage per hour. How does this differ from Reserved Instances?

options.text: Savings Plans are more expensive than Reserved Instances
Savings Plans offer flexibility across instance types and services; Reserved Instances are tied to a specific instance type and region
Reserved Instances can apply to Lambda; Savings Plans cannot
There is no functional difference — they are equivalent products

explanation.correct: Compute Savings Plans apply to any EC2 instance family, size, region, OS, or tenancy — and also cover Lambda and Fargate. Reserved Instances are tied to a specific instance type in a specific region (Standard RI) or instance family (Convertible RI).
explanation.why: Savings Plans trade slightly lower maximum discount for much greater architectural flexibility as your workload evolves.

questions.question: Termination protection is enabled on an EC2 instance. A user with full EC2 AdministratorAccess IAM permissions tries to terminate it. What happens?

options.text: The instance is terminated because IAM permissions override termination protection
AWS prompts for MFA before terminating
The termination is blocked — the user must first disable termination protection
The instance moves to Stopping state instead of Terminated

explanation.correct: Termination protection is an instance-level attribute that blocks the terminate action regardless of IAM permissions. The user must explicitly disable termination protection before they can terminate the instance.
explanation.why: This is a deliberate defense-in-depth design — even admins cannot accidentally terminate protected instances without a two-step process.

questions.question: You reboot an EC2 instance. Which of the following is TRUE?

options.text: The instance gets a new public IP address after reboot
The root EBS volume is deleted on reboot
The instance retains its public IP and stays on the same physical host
Rebooting is equivalent to stop then start

explanation.correct: Reboot is an in-place restart on the same physical host. The instance retains its public and private IP addresses, its instance ID, and all data on its attached volumes.
explanation.why: Stop/Start can move the instance to different physical hardware and releases the public IP. Reboot does neither.

questions.question: An EC2 instance's 'Instance initiated shutdown behavior' is set to 'Terminate'. A developer runs 'sudo shutdown -h now' from inside the instance. What happens?

options.text: The instance stops and can be restarted
The instance moves to Terminated state permanently
AWS blocks the shutdown and logs a security event

explanation.correct: When the shutdown behavior is set to Terminate, any OS-level shutdown command causes the instance to be permanently terminated — not just stopped.
explanation.why: This is why production instances should always have this setting on Stop. An accidental sudo shutdown -h now would otherwise permanently delete the server.

questions.question: Which combination of features provides the STRONGEST protection against accidental permanent loss of a production EC2 instance?

options.text: Termination protection + IAM policies restricting terminate action + regular AMI backups
Setting instance shutdown behavior to Stop only

explanation.correct: Defence in depth: termination protection blocks accidental console clicks, IAM policies restrict who can even attempt termination, and AMI backups ensure you can recover even if termination somehow occurs.
explanation.why: No single feature is sufficient alone — layering protections creates true resilience.

questions.question: You have a 3-node web application cluster running on EC2. You want to upgrade one node from t3.medium to c5.xlarge. What is the minimum downtime required?

options.text: Zero downtime — you can change instance type while running
The node must be stopped, type changed, then started — expect 2-5 minutes offline for that node
The entire cluster must be stopped simultaneously
You must terminate and re-launch with the new type

explanation.correct: Changing instance type requires a stop/start cycle for that specific instance — typically 2-5 minutes. The other nodes remain running, so the cluster keeps serving traffic (with one fewer node temporarily).
explanation.why: This is exactly why load balancers and multi-node architectures matter — they absorb the downtime of individual node maintenance.

questions.question: Which EC2 pricing model offers the MOST flexibility but at the HIGHEST cost?

explanation.correct: On-Demand is pay-as-you-go with no commitments — maximum flexibility but maximum per-unit cost. All other models trade some flexibility for lower prices.
explanation.why: On-Demand is the baseline price that all other models are discounted against.

questions.question: A company has an Oracle database with a per-physical-core license. Which EC2 hosting model allows them to track and control how many physical cores their Oracle instance uses?

explanation.correct: Dedicated Hosts give visibility into the underlying physical server's socket and core layout, which is required for per-core and per-socket software licensing compliance such as Oracle or Microsoft SQL Server.
explanation.why: On-Demand, Reserved, and Spot instances are multi-tenant — the physical server is shared with other customers and you do not control core allocation.

questions.question: An instance is in the 'Shutting-down' state. Can you start it again?

options.text: Yes, by clicking Start in the console within 5 minutes
Yes, but only via the AWS CLI
No — Shutting-down transitions to Terminated which is irreversible
Yes, but only if termination protection was previously enabled

explanation.correct: Shutting-down is a brief transition state that always leads to Terminated — it cannot be reversed. Once Terminated, the instance is permanently gone.
explanation.why: This is why termination protection is critical — once the terminate action executes, there is no recovery path.

questions.question: Which statement about EC2 Instance Connect is CORRECT?

options.text: It works for both Linux and Windows EC2 instances
It requires the .pem key file to be uploaded into the browser
It injects a temporary one-time key and requires port 22 open in the Security Group
It bypasses Security Group rules for convenience

explanation.correct: EC2 Instance Connect pushes a temporary one-time SSH public key to the instance for 60 seconds and then removes it. Port 22 must still be open in the Security Group.
explanation.why: It does not work for Windows (RDP), does not require your .pem file, and does NOT bypass Security Groups.
